reasoning: MSA-origin word that Palestinians use freely in conversation. ث is said as s here, and the tanween an is pronounced.
ق is a glottal stop in everyday 'abl. The hamza after the prefix il- is written, as in il-'usbuu3. wala means 'or' here, and -o is 'it/him' on ba3do.
Country name with the article, said il-meksiik. The first vowel is e or i, so I am not fully certain of it.
In the construct state taa marbuta becomes t: kilmit. ق in 7a' is a glottal stop as in everyday speech, though the phrase is somewhat proverbial.
Formal or written conjunction; ay becomes ee if it is said at all. In speech Palestinians use wa't ma or lamma for 'while', a circumstantial w-, or bass for contrast.
Taa marbuta after ز is e: jaayze. The word means just 'prize'; 'grand prize' would be il-jaayze il-kubra.
ay becomes long ee in Palestinian: 3een. Standard word for eye.
Palestinian 'where', with long ee, as in the dialect rules.
English loanword in daily use, written with ف so said with f. The exact vowel of the first syllable varies between speakers.
Common Levantine idiom, literally 'hit two birds with a stone', used for 'killed two birds with one stone'. ض, ص and ع are written as in the scheme; 3aSfuur could also be said 3uSfuur.
'Accept' is an everyday verb, so ق is a glottal stop. The 2nd-person plural ends in -u, and بس is said bass with a doubled s. The loanword cash is kaash.
Form V verb with a doubled s, used in everyday speech for improving or recovering.
Form I past, he-form. It also means to withdraw money.
Form V, with a doubled glottal stop from ق. Urban speakers usually glottalise ق even in this MSA-origin verb, though some would say tawaqqa3.
In Palestinian speech شراب also means socks, usually as a collective or plural, said with an initial cluster. The drink is sharaab, so context decides.
Standard word for eagle or vulture, said nasr. 3uqaab is also used for eagle.
The hamza and h are not pronounced in speech: inshaalla. khayr becomes kheer. A natural reply when someone brings worrying or unexpected news.
2nd-person masculine present with the bi- prefix, plus shu for 'what'. It is used as 'guess what' or 'you know what'.
Form V verb with emphatic ط written T and a doubled w. MSA-origin but used in conversation.

meaning_fix: how are you, my dear (lit. my heart)
reasoning: The Hebron tag does not apply to Ramallah, where ق is a glottal stop: 'albi. Hebron speakers say k for ق. The phrase itself is a normal affectionate greeting to a man.
Emphatic ط is T. Taa marbuta after ي is e: 3aafye. A standard thanks to someone who is working, said to a man.
Levantine speech usually shortens the first vowel, giving ijaar rather than MSA iijaar. I am not fully sure of the length.
The country name is normally spelled بولندا and said boolanda. The given spelling lacks the و, so I respelled it to match what is said.
Loanword, usually spelled بيجامة. Taa marbuta after م is e by the scheme, so bijaame.
Active-participle shape, with a long aa and short i: shaarib. Standard word for mustache; the plural is shawaarib.
